subject: Damascus steel sword
title: A 400-Year-Old Sword Contains Carbon Nanotubes, and Nobody Knows How

scenes.text: A sword forged 400 years ago is full of nanotechnology.
Damascus steel. Blades said to bend from hilt to tip and cut a falling silk scarf in half.
In 2006, researchers in Dresden dissolved part of a 17th-century sabre in acid and put it under an electron microscope.
Inside: carbon nanotubes, each about half a nanometre wide. Ten million would fit on the head of a thumbtack.
The secret seems to be trace metals in Indian ore, like vanadium. When those mines ran out in the 1700s, the recipe died.
No smith since has reproduced it. A medieval sword with the tech of the 21st century.

description:
A sword forged 400 years ago is full of nanotechnology.
In 2006 Marianne Reibold and colleagues at the University of Dresden dissolved part of a 17th-century Damascus sabre by the smith Assad Ullah in hydrochloric acid and examined it under an electron microscope. They found carbon nanotubes just over half a nanometre wide wrapped around nanowires of cementite, which may explain how the high-carbon steel was both hard and flexible. The researchers believe trace metals such as vanadium in Indian wootz ore made the structures form; when those ores ran out in the 18th century, the art was lost and no smith has fully reproduced it.
Which lost ancient technology would you most like to see rediscovered?
first_comment: The steel had about 1.5 percent carbon, which should make it brittle. Instead it bent. Which ancient object do you think hides modern science?
